narrative:
The model predicted a 97% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission based on predicted first-time success, this high probability of failure led directly to the rejection of your application.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your class rank in the third year of law school, your LSAT score, and your first-year class rank. All three pushed the prediction strongly toward failure rather than success.

Your third-year ranking placed you in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average student who is admitted. This was the single most influential piece of information the model considered. Your LSAT score of 23.5 was also substantially lower than the average of 37 among accepted students, giving the model further reason to expect difficulty passing the bar. Finally, your first-year ranking in the lowest decile reinforced the same pattern of academic struggle.

Your low undergraduate GPA of 2.10 compared with an average of 3.23 among accepted students added supporting evidence, though it carried less weight than the three factors above. Your family income, gender, race, and full-time status played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake classes, consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score significantly, and explore bar-preparation programs that have strong track records with students who start from a similar position. These steps can demonstrably change your outlook for future applications. (248 words)
